reason: The chambers need muscle to squeeze and drive blood forward.
expectation: The heart muscle will surround the chambers so they can contract.

effect: The muscular chambers can squeeze, but fluid moves toward both openings, so the pump still needs one-way control.
reaction: The two-way arrows make the remaining problem clear.
reason: The valve picture suggests they will prevent reverse flow during a squeeze.
expectation: The valves will guide blood forward by closing against reverse flow.

effect: The valves direct flow forward during a squeeze and allow the chambers to refill.
reaction: The squeeze and refill panels make the valves' roles clear.
reason: The pacemaker cells appear to provide the electrical signals needed for repeated squeezes.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will give the heart a repeating contraction rhythm.

effect: The pacemaker completes the beating pump; the remaining goal is to fit it and blood into a returning route.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it is useful.
reason: Hemoglobin has oxygen-binding sites, so it should give the red-cell envelopes their oxygen-carrying function.
expectation: The envelopes and hemoglobin will form oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

effect: The red blood cells can carry oxygen and make ATP from sugar despite lacking nuclei and mitochondria. They now need to join the blood route.
reaction: The contrast with the muscle cells is interesting.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The cells and plasma will form blood.

effect: The red blood cells and plasma form oxygen-carrying blood, with sugar dissolved in the plasma. The remaining task is to connect the pump and blood to a returning vessel route.
reaction: The picture makes the different locations of hemoglobin and sugar clear.
reason: The arteries and veins need capillary networks to connect their branching routes.
expectation: The vessels and capillaries will form a connected route for blood to travel out and return.

effect: The capillaries connect the outward and returning vessels, leaving slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The empty slots make the remaining assembly clear.
reason: The beating heart fits the circuit's pump slot.
expectation: The beating heart will be fitted into the vessel circuit as its pump.

effect: The beating heart is fitted into the circuit; the transport medium slot remains.
reaction: The heart’s connection to both outgoing and returning vessels is clear.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the remaining transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will be fitted into the vessel circuit.

effect: Adding blood completed the circuit. The final pictures show exchange with tissue cells and blood returning to circulate again.
reaction: Seeing the separate pieces become a returning route was satisfying; the capillary inset also clarified that red cells stay inside the vessels.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the valves was most worthwhile: the before-and-after pictures made it clear why squeezing alone does not ensure forward flow, and the refill panel showed the other half of the cycle.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart into the named pump slot felt like straightforward assembly. It was clear, but added less to my understanding than building the pump itself.

surprise.text: I was interested that red blood cells lack nuclei and mitochondria yet still make ATP from sugar in their fluid. That contrasted with the muscle cells built earlier.

arbitrary.text: None felt arbitrary. The pictures and goal supplied a practical reason for each combination, although the final fittings were predictable.

continue.text: Yes. I would be curious to see how the circuit connects to other body systems, since the final result says it serves many tissues.
